profile.summary: Ezra narrates God's sovereign act by bringing back part of his Babylonian exile people to Jerusalem, restore worship and confront sin that threatened the holy identity of the community. The book shows returns, external opposition, temple reconstruction, instruction by the Law and, finally, repentance before marriages to pagan peoples. To the evangelical reader, Ezra shows that the restoration of God's people depends on divine providence, fidelity to the Word and a real separation from sin.
profile.setting: The backdrop begins with the fall of Judah, about 130 years before Ezra's arrival in Jerusalem in 458 BC: Babylon destroys the city, breaks down the temple, and deports the people. In exile, Jews live relatively stable, but far from the promised land. With the rise of the Persian Empire, Cyrus allows the return in 538 BC, and the book follows the story from 538 to about 450 BC. The return takes place in the midst of a land already occupied by other peoples brought by the previous empires, which generates conflict and pressure by religious mixing. Authorship is traditionally attributed to Ezra, sometimes along with Nehemiah, but this identification is debated; the source also highlights that the book preserves official documents in Hebrew and Aramaic, reinforcing its historical character.

structure.label: First return and beginning of restoration
structure.description: Cyrus' decree allows the return of the exiles; the people re-erce the community, establish the altar and begin the reconstruction of the temple, facing local opposition and the refusal of religious commitments.

structure.label: Reactivation and conclusion of the temple
structure.description: Years later, the prophets encourage the people to resume the work, and the temple is finally completed with Persian support and without further interference.

structure.label: Arrival of Esdras and preparation for reform
structure.description: Ezra arrives with authority to administer the affairs of the people and receive the necessary resources; the text highlights its mission of teaching and applying the Law.

structure.label: Confession and renewal of the alliance
structure.description: Ezra discovers infidelity in marriages with foreigners, intercedes in favor of the people and leads the community to repentance and separation from sin.

themes: Purity of God's people and separation from sin
The value of intercessory prayer and confession
readingKeys: Notice how the text attributes to God the initiative behind real decrees, protection and provision.
Note the tension between physical restoration (temple, community) and spiritual restoration (obedience, holiness).
Follow the function of lists, documents and decrees: they serve to legitimize the restoration and show order under divine providence.
profile.cautions: The source presents traditional authorship cautiously, but records that many scholars contest broader connections with Chronicles; the date and historical organization also involve reconstruction from internal documents and references. The introduction interprets mixed marriages as a threat to fidelity to the covenant, but the reader should avoid reading the book as mere administrative account: his focus is theological, showing restoration, holiness and repentance under the rule of God.

dossier.narratedEra: The book narrates the restoration of Judah after Babylonian exile, covering from Cyrus' decree in 538 BC until the time of Ezra in Jerusalem, around 458 BC, with the mention of events linked to opposition and reconstruction extending to about 445 BC in the immediate backdrop of the restored community.
dossier.compositionEra: The notes presented traditionally associate Ezra and Nehemiah as one book written by Ezra, who would have access to many official documents preserved in the text. They also record a traditional proposal that Ezra would have written Chronicles by similarity between 2 Chronicles 36:22-23 and Ezra 1:1-3, but observe that many scholars reject this conclusion and see important linguistic and theological differences. The sources provided do not accurately date the final composition.

politics.title: Persian rule replaces Babylon
politics.detail: Cyrus II reigns in Persia from 559 to 530 BC, and the Persians defeat Babylon in 539 BC, paving the way for the return of the exiles. Reading gains a focus on God's sovereignty over empires, not just about religious leaders.
politics.readingImpact: The return is not presented as a political accident, but as God-directed action through empire changes.

politics.title: Persian imperial policy of repatriation
politics.detail: The notes contrast the Assyrian-babyonic policy of deportation and dispersion with Persian, which allowed the exiles to return to their lands to be grateful, obedient and pay tributes. This helps to understand why Cyrus' decree is politically plausible in the Persian world.
politics.readingImpact: The restoration of Jerusalem takes place within an imperial strategy of control and loyalty, not outside international politics.

politics.title: Ciro's function in rebuilding the temple
politics.detail: Cyrus is described as a monarch who, though pagan, is moved by God to issue a decree for the construction of the temple in Jerusalem. The note also suggests that the proclamation had political value and could function as propaganda to raise Jewish support for his government.
politics.readingImpact: The community must read the decree as an instrument of divine providence, without romanticizing the piety of the Persian king.

politics.title: Persian authorities and local supervision
politics.detail: In 5:3, the question about who authorized the work is treated as a routine inquiry to verify that everything was in accordance with the official requirements. In 5:6-17, Tatenai and other officers appear as inspectors/researchers of the empire.
politics.readingImpact: The reader sees reconstruction as subject to the imperial bureaucracy; the fidelity of the people must operate within real administrative structures.

politics.title: Management of local governors and leaders
politics.detail: The note about 1:8 identifies Sesbazar as governor appointed by the Persians and suggests that he began the temple work, while Zorobabel possibly concluded it later. Local politics thus appears mediated by leaders appointed by the empire.
politics.readingImpact: The reconstruction does not depend on a single heroic character; it goes through succession of leaders under Persian supervision.

customs.title: Possible life in Babylonian exile
customs.detail: The notes say that the exiles in Babylon could build houses, have gardens and live relatively well, with some religious freedom; some also came to positions of power. This shows that the return was not motivated by pure material need.
customs.readingImpact: The cost of the return appears higher: whoever comes out of a stable life does so for fidelity, not for convenience.
customs.reference: context of Jeremiah 29 cited in the introductory notes

customs.title: Voluntary offer and transportation of sacred objects
customs.detail: On the initial return, there were voluntary donations for the work and transport of temple utensils. The notes emphasize that these objects were sacred and very valuable, and that their count and preservation distinguished the saint of the profane.
customs.readingImpact: Restoration involves careful administration of worship, not just spiritual enthusiasm.

customs.title: Lists of Community identity
customs.detail: The lists of those who returned with Zerubbabel and Ezra are interpreted as a way to ensure who could participate in the worship and the holy community. The official records protected the border between those belonging and non-participating.
customs.readingImpact: Genealogy and documentation become part of community holiness, and not mere bureaucratic detail.

customs.title: Marriage with foreigners and family separation
customs.detail: In 10:3, the note defines the covenant as a commitment to divorce the pagan women, and adds that, in the case of marital breakage, women usually received the custody of their children. This shows the social and familiar weight of the decision.
customs.readingImpact: The text does not only deal with abstract doctrine; it reaches homes, children and concrete ruptures.

customs.title: Fasting, lament and public meeting under rain
customs.detail: Ezra tears the garments, weeps and fasts; then the assembly takes place on a cold and rainy day. Notes highlight the physical discomfort and public sincerity of confession.
customs.readingImpact: Reading gains body dimension: repentance involves visible grief and real discomfort, not only speech.

language.title: Aramaic as imperial language
language.detail: The book contains two sections in Aramaic, the common language of the Persian empire, and six official documents appear in them. This marks the alternation between Hebrew narrative and imperial administrative documentation.
language.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the history of restoration is anchored in official archives, not just in devotional narrative.

language.title: Documental value of lists and decrees
language.detail: The notes highlight that Ezra includes decrees, utensil lists, returned lists, treasures and names of those who divorced from pagan wives. These materials serve as proof of precision and distinction between the saint and the non-holy.
language.readingImpact: The documentary style reinforces the historical credibility and the theme of religious separation.

language.title: The God of heaven as an intelligible title to the Persians
language.detail: The expression is explained as a Persian way of referring to the supreme and universal God, not to a smaller local divinity. The same observation appears both in the decree of Cyrus and in the letter linked to Tatenai.
language.readingImpact: The diplomatic language shows that Israel's faith is being communicated into intelligible categories in the imperial environment.

language.title: Great king and the memory of Solomon
language.detail: In 5:11, the expression "Great King of Israel" is explained as a reference to Solomon. The note connects the work of post-exile with the former glory of the kingdom.
language.readingImpact: The comparison with Solomon makes the reader measure the current reconstruction by the memory of the ancient temple.

language.title: Language of grief and confession
language.detail: The note about 10:1 insists that Ezra's mourning was genuine and produced an answer in others. In 9:6-15, his prayer is presented as a model of humility and intercession.
language.readingImpact: Emotional language is not ornamentation; it describes the environment by which the community is confronted and renewed.

timeline.title: Fall of Babylon and beginning of return
timeline.detail: Cyrus defeats Babylon in 539 BC; in 538 BC he allows the exit of the Jews. The first group led by Sesbazar returns to the land.
timeline.readingImpact: The restoration begins as a fulfillment of prophetic promise, not as a mere political readjustment.

timeline.title: First phase of the restored community
timeline.detail: Between 538 and 536 BC, the returnees reorganize the community, build the altar and begin the temple, but the local opposition interrupts the work.
timeline.readingImpact: The cult resumes before the completion of the building, showing liturgical priority and social vulnerability.

timeline.title: Resumption of temple construction under Hageu and Zechariah
timeline.detail: He prophesied in August 520 BC and Zechariah about two months later; these prophets propell the resumption of the work, which culminates in the completion of the temple in 515 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: The chronology shows that prophetic perseverance was decisive in passing through the previous stagnation.

timeline.title: Persian investigations and correspondence
timeline.detail: Tatenai's letter to Darius is treated as an official verification of the legality of the work, and the imperial response confirms the advance. The notes highlight the documentary character of this period.
timeline.readingImpact: The reconstruction of the temple is carried out by imperial approval, not just by local decision.

timeline.title: Ezra arrives in Jerusalem
timeline.detail: In 458 BC, Ezra goes to Jerusalem to administer government affairs and find the problem of marriages to foreigners.
timeline.readingImpact: The second major stage of the book shifts the focus of building the temple to the moral reform of the community.

timeline.title: The crisis of mixed marriages and the response of the community
timeline.detail: After Ezra's prayer, official judicial investigation takes place, repentance and separation of pagan wives; the note mentions 10:44 as the closure of the list of those involved. The process is treated as restoration of the covenant.
timeline.readingImpact: The outcome shows that the purity of the community is maintained by confession, discipline, and obedience.

investigation: The aforementioned notes strongly emphasize the sovereignty of God, the purity of the people and the authority of Scripture, in evangelical-protestant reading, but without erasing the Persian imperial context and documentary bureaucracy.

There is a traditional and academic divergence on authorship and relationship with Chronicles: the sources record the tradition of Ezra's authorship and the hypothesis of having also written Chronicles, but report that many scholars reject this latter conclusion.

Some historical statements appear as an interpretation of the notes, not as independent external proof; for example, the reading of Cyrus' decree as political propaganda and the identification of certain Persian administrative structures.
The coverage provided is selective: it illuminates mainly 1, 4-5, 7-10, with few direct observations about details of everyday life outside of exile, travel and assembly of repentance.
The sources also do not solve all the internal chronological debates of the book; therefore, the dates here are restricted to those explicitly given or inferred by the attached notes themselves.

This dossier depends solely on the annexed notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry, without resorting to other sources, harmonizations or historical reconstructions of their own. Therefore, it does not include information that the material does not mention clearly, nor does it attempt to fill gaps with general query data. Sections about politics, customs, language, and chronology reflect only what notes directly discuss or what they explicitly affirm. Some points are interpretative, especially when the note evaluates political, religious or editorial motivations; in these cases, the classification as interpretation indicates inference of the grades themselves, not independent proof. There are also unresolved controversies in the material provided, such as the authorship of Chronicles and the exact extent of the final composition of Ezra-Nehemiah. The dossier privileges the historical-cultural context that alters devotional and exegetical reading, but recognizes that not every dimension of the book was covered in the attached notes.
